title: NVIDIA opens three Nemotron 3.5 Parse datasets and a fine-tuning recipe, with DFlash2 inference 7.62x faster
summary: If you use models to turn scans, PDFs, or charts into structured data, NVIDIA has now released the Nemotron 3.5 Parse training data and fine-tuning recipe, plus a DFlash2 acceleration option: on a single H200, throughput at concurrency 1 improves 7.62x.
ai_summary: NVIDIA has open-sourced three things after Nemotron 3.5 Parse: three synthetic training datasets (9.98M chart examples, 1M table examples, 7.9M multilingual OCR examples), an SFT + RLVR fine-tuning recipe, and a speculative-decoding accelerator called DFlash2. Training first uses supervised fine-tuning to teach the model to read pages, then reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to improve consistency: looped outputs drop from 126 to 29 pages, and total score rises from 66.24 to 71.38. On a single H200 in BF16, DFlash2 improves throughput 7.62x at concurrency 1 and reaches 20.44 pages/s at concurrency 512. The most practical part is applying the recipe to your own documents: in NVIDIA's example, first-attempt success on a dental form goes from 0.00% to 96.58%. These are NVIDIA's own evaluation numbers; verify them on your own data.
brief: The three open datasets cover 9.98M chart examples, 1M table examples, and 7.9M multilingual OCR examples, including images, annotations, and training format.
In a matched comparison, RLVR cuts looped outputs from 126 pages to 29 and lifts the overall score from 66.24 to 71.38.
On a single H200 in BF16, DFlash2 delivers 7.62x throughput at concurrency 1 and 20.44 pages/s at concurrency 512.
Dental-form fine-tuning example: first-attempt success rises from 0.00% to 96.58%; the recipe is open, so you can apply it to your own documents.

cover.headline: Nemotron Parse opens further
cover.highlight: Open data, a fine-tuning recipe, and faster inference

sections.h: What it is: turning a page into structured data with labels and bounding boxes

blocks.p: Nemotron 3.5 Parse is NVIDIA's document parser: feed it a scanned page or PDF image and it arranges the content in reading order, assigns each block a type such as heading, paragraph, table, or chart, and returns a bounding box — the coordinates for the rectangular area the content occupies. Tables and charts also become structured records you can use for RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: pull relevant content from a document, then let a model answer from it) or feed to agents.

This post follows the model release with three additions: open synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe you can copy, and DFlash2 for faster inference. The point is that the data and the method are both open, so others can train their own document models the same way.

blocks.p: All three datasets are synthetic: rather than hand-labeling real scans, NVIDIA rendered charts, tables, and multilingual pages programmatically. Because the generator knows each bar's value and each cell's content, the ground truth is exact by construction, and fonts, layouts, and languages can be varied to increase diversity.

items.label: Synthetic Tables V1
items.note: HTML tables with rows, columns, and headers preserved

blocks.p: Each dataset includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. NVIDIA suggests either fine-tuning a document model directly or following the same method to generate new variants for a specific document type or language.
The community has already extended Parse to Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic; releasing this data and recipe is meant to help more people do similar work.

sections.h: Why chart and table parsing got better

blocks.p: The most obvious gains in this release are on charts and tables, especially hard or ambiguous cases. Many bar and line charts have no printed numbers, so the model has to infer values from axes and bar heights; the post gives an example where Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from a chart's geometry.

Tables are trickier because the structure itself carries meaning: one shifted row or column changes the interpretation of the whole table. These gains mostly come from synthetic data — render charts and tables with known ground truth, then have the model reverse the process, like a controlled workbook of exercises.

callout.title: Why synthetic data fits charts and tables especially well
callout.text: Labeling values in real documents by hand is slow, expensive, and error-prone. With rendered images, every bar value and cell content is already known, so you can automatically generate large numbers of examples with exact answers.

sections.h: Two-stage training: SFT builds the skill, RLVR improves consistency

blocks.p: Training happens in two steps. First, SFT (supervised fine-tuning): the model gets page-plus-correct-structured-output pairs and learns to read a page and represent its contents. This stage covers text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents to build the core ability.

Second, RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards), optimized with GRPO. The model samples outputs, then automatically checkable rules score them: did the chart recover the right series and values? Is the structure usable? Did it repeat the same content? A hard page can have many valid representations, so the reward does not force one exact answer; it rewards correct and complete output and penalizes looping and unfinished work.

fig.title: RLVR cuts looping, trims overlong outputs, and raises the total score
fig.subtitle: Development checkpoints: SFT vs. GRPO in matched settings; amber marks GRPO values
fig.note: Source uses development checkpoints, not the final released model; loops are counted with a repetition check

blocks.p: The post gives a matched comparison: looped outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages, about 77% fewer; outputs hitting the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35 pages; total score rises from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points on tables and +4.15 on charts. Note these are development checkpoints, not the final released model.

sections.h: DFlash2 speeds inference: architecture changes plus a small draft model

blocks.p: A parsing model emits a lot of text and structure for every page, which is compute-hungry. Parse 3.5 makes four architecture changes; the figure below compares it with Parse 2.0.

fig.title: Parse 3.5 swaps a fixed canvas for page-adaptive input
fig.subtitle: Amber marks the changes this time

items.label: Compressed visual tokens as a causal prefix

blocks.p: The most interesting part is speculative decoding: a small draft model guesses what comes next, and the large model verifies the guesses in one pass; correct guesses save time. The built-in MTP head only looks ahead 1 token, while DFlash2 is a more powerful draft model that can guess up to 32 tokens ahead, which Parse verifies together. In the measured 32-token configuration, about 14 draft tokens are accepted on average, so each verification advances roughly 15 output tokens including the target token.

On a single H200 in BF16 on the same 2,078-page benchmark, DFlash2 improves throughput by 7.62x at concurrency 1 and 1.52x at concurrency 512. In absolute terms at concurrency 512, Parse 3.5 without speculation runs at 13.48 pages/s, with DFlash2 at 20.44 pages/s, and Parse 2.0 only 2.98 pages/s. That is 4.53x and 6.86x over Parse 2.0, respectively.

fig.title: At concurrency 512, DFlash2 lifts throughput from 13.48 to 20.44 pages/s
fig.subtitle: Units: pages/s; single H200, BF16, same 2,078 pages; amber shows DFlash2

sections.h: When one pass is not enough, double or triple pass re-reads hard regions

blocks.p: Faster inference leaves room to re-read difficult regions. Single-pass parsing reads the whole page once and outputs text, layout, tables, and charts. Double-pass takes the table and chart regions found on the first pass, crops and enlarges them, parses them again, and merges the refinements back. Triple-pass adds a detection mode that verifies all boxes are found and no text is missed, then re-reads the charts and tables it found.

fig.title: If one pass is not enough, crop the hard regions and read them again
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: amber marks steps added in multi-pass parsing; scores from NVIDIA's reference evaluation

items.label: Outputs text, layout, tables, and charts in one pass
Double: crops and enlarges table and chart regions for re-reading
Triple: adds a detection mode to confirm boxes and text

blocks.p: In NVIDIA's reference evaluation, double pass scores 2.18 ParseBench points higher than single pass, and triple pass 2.46 points higher. The tradeoff is that multiple crops mean multiple requests, so throughput drops — essentially trading speed for accuracy on hard regions.

callout.title: Speed and quality can be tuned separately
callout.text: DFlash2 addresses speed; double/triple parsing addresses accuracy on hard regions. The two can be combined: use multi-pass parsing to raise quality, then use DFlash2 to claw back the extra compute.

sections.h: The fine-tuning recipe: a dental form example

blocks.p: NVIDIA's recipe is a pipeline: pair your own images with gold labels, run SFT with NeMo Automodel, then run RLVR with GRPO in NeMo RL, using vLLM to generate candidate answers. You also need a verifier to decide whether an extraction is correct. The built-in document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion; combine the ones your task needs and add your own schema checks.

The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram — a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before fine-tuning, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the planned procedure table; after SFT, it learns to link each marked tooth to a procedure and position. The post says all six chart rows match the target after SFT.

On an evaluation of 256 held-out forms from the same generator, with 8 samples per page, the first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1 — correct on the first sample) rises from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR. Success means natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text.

fig.title: Dental form: first-attempt success from 0 to 96.58%
fig.subtitle: 256 held-out forms, 8 samples per page; success = completion + chart match + clean text; unit: %

list: License details for the three datasets and the recipe are not listed separately; check the corresponding model and dataset pages before using them.
The fine-tuning demo is only shown on synthetic data; the dental example itself comes from the same synthetic generator, so performance on real, heterogeneous scans is unknown.
DFlash2 throughput is tested only on a single H200 in BF16; other GPUs, precisions, and higher concurrency are not reported.
Double/triple parsing only reports score gains (+2.18, +2.46), with no numbers for extra requests or throughput loss.
Pricing is not mentioned: the model and datasets are open, but you will need to calculate GPU costs for self-hosted inference.

blocks.p: The value: if you need to turn scans, PDFs, receipts, medical records, or forms into structured data, the open data and recipe save you from starting from scratch, with chart/table parsing and multilingual OCR as ready-made starting points. DFlash2's 7.62x gain at concurrency 1 is more pronounced than at high concurrency.
The cost: you need to prepare paired data, write a verifier, and run training yourself; the numbers in the post are NVIDIA's own benchmarks and development checkpoints, not a general guarantee.

list: If you are building RAG or a document agent: start by running Parse 3.5 directly and see if it is good enough before deciding to fine-tune.
If you have a specific format such as dental forms, invoices, or contracts: follow the recipe with SFT + RLVR; it is less work than training from scratch.
If you process low-concurrency or single documents: turn on DFlash2 first; the gain shrinks at high batch concurrency but remains faster than Parse 2.0.
If documents are hard, such as dense tables or small charts: use double or triple pass, trading throughput for accuracy.
